items.note: By extension a house, a shelter: sub tēctō, indoors.

example.la: Sub hoc ille tecto tam sordido stetit

traps.reply: That's a city or defensive wall. The wall of a house is pariēs.

example.la: si enim nihil est in parietibus aut in tecto viti
fenestrarum angustias quod reprehendis

traps.reply: That's clāvus, the nail. A key is clāvis, -is (f.).

example.la: ex duodecim tabulis clavis ademit, exegit.
cardines in foribus diutius immoti

items.note: Plural only. Also a staircase.

example.la: scalis vallum ascendere coeperunt.
lapides congerentem in situlam monimenti
vel cum cinis in foco concrescit
non aliter quam scintilla flatu levi adiuta ignem suum explicat
Graeci enim in conviviis solent nominare, cui poculum tradituri sint.

items.note: exhaurīre: to draw off to the last drop.

example.la: poculum exhausit.

traps.reply: That's clāvis, the key. A nail is clāvus, -ī (m.).

example.la: confixa clavis ferreis digiti pollicis crassitudine

items.note: pangere stands in the old law Livy quotes (7.3.5).

example.la: ea religione adductus senatus dictatorem clavi figendi causa dici iussit.

traps.reply: That's a cliff. Rope is fūnis, -is (m.).

example.la: cum essent funibus, ancoris reliquisque armamentis amissis ad navigandum inutiles
Notabile erat iugum adstrictum compluribus nodis in semetipsos inplicatis et celantibus nexus.
hamumque de cubiculo ac paene etiam de lectulo ut e naucula iacere.

items.note: From cubāre, to lie down.

example.la: ubi in vicinia cubiti umerus fractus est

items.note: Also envy.

traps.reply: That's the English word. The mark a blow leaves is līvor, -ōris (m.).

example.la: Quod si facie contusa livor subcruentus est

traps.reply: That's hide, leather. The bark of a tree is cortex, -icis (m.).

example.la: prius se cortice ex arboribus victuros, quam Pompeium e manibus dimissuros.

items.note: Also the backbone.

example.la: sed eius generis, quod spinas non habet

traps.reply: That's a stone of any size. A pebble is its diminutive, lapillus; calculus too.

example.la: correptisque opperiri lapillis, mobilitatem pondere stabilientes

items.note: Columella sets plūma, the soft plumage of the body, beside pinnae, the wing and tail feathers (8.2.7).

example.la: penna vulturina subiecta pedibus adiuvat parturientes.

items.note: Also a feather as the type of lightness: plūmā aut foliō facilius (Cic. Att. 8.15.2).

example.la: hoc tenui pluma completum dolium ore in cuniculum verso posuerunt.
quem in luto volutatum totius corporis vestigiis invenimus?

items.note: dē caelō tangī is the formula in lists of prodigies.

traps.reply: capere is to seize. Lightning strikes or touches: fulmine īcī, fulmine tangī.

example.la: Romulus lactens fulmine ictus

traps.reply: The verb with fidem is servāre, or praestāre.

example.la: secundum ea quaero servarisne in eo fidem?
ad supplicium redire maluit quam fidem hosti datam fallere.

items.note: Deponent. With accusative and future infinitive.

example.la: pollicitusque est sibi eam rem curae futuram

items.note: Both halves decline: iūre iūrandō.

example.la: sed ius iurandum conservandum putabat.

items.note: With accusative and future infinitive.

example.la: tenentem iurare iussit numquam me in amicitia cum Romanis fore.

items.note: With an infinitive. dēcernere is the word for an official decree.

example.la: ipse cum tribus legionibus circum Samarobrivam trinis hibernis hiemare constituit

items.note: Followed by ut or an infinitive. It also serves for “to decide”.

example.la: subito consilium cepi ut ante quam luceret exirem

items.note: sententia is the view you hold; mēns the whole bent of mind: mūtātā mente (Sall. Cat. 48.1).

example.la: mutare sententiam turpe est

items.note: With ad and the accusative. Animum advertere works too, but leans toward noticing; animum intendere is to bend the mind to a task.

example.la: praesertim cum animum attendisset ad cavendum.
non ergo perdamus primum statim tempus

items.prompt: to take advantage of an opportunity
items.note: ūtī takes the ablative. Caesar has ūtī temporis opportūnitāte (BC 2.34.4).

example.la: sed occasione vincendi strenue est usus.

traps.reply: That's to be in danger. To go to meet it is perīculum subīre, or adīre.

example.la: Sic et ad subeundum periculum et ad vitandum multum fortuna valuit.

items.note: With dē and the ablative, or an accusative.

example.la: Aut cur de sua virtute aut de ipsius diligentia desperarent?

items.note: With the accusative. With the dative it means to look after someone's interests.

traps.reply: With the dative, cōnsulere is to look after someone. To ask advice it takes the accusative: aliquem cōnsulere.

example.la: te consulo, qui philosophum audis

items.note: With the dative of the person.

traps.reply: With agere it is plural: grātiās agere.

example.la: Terentia tibi et saepe et maximas agit gratias.

items.note: Dative of the person wronged, genitive of the offence.

traps.reply: The idiom is plural: poenās dare.

example.la: quam ipsum aliquando poenas dare.

items.note: With the dative: fīnitimīs bellum īnferre.

traps.reply: ingerere is to heap upon. War is carried against someone: bellum īnferre.

example.la: et minus facile finitimis bellum inferre possent
cohortatus suos proelium commisit.
iuxtaque murum castra posuit.
ab confluente Rhodam castra movi

items.note: Of troops falling back before the enemy.

example.la: barbari constiterunt ac paulum modo pedem rettulerunt.
